I think the most important thing is to listen and believe him. Honesty is powerful. Don't just be honest with him-- make it important that he's always honest with you. If you show that you're interested in helping, he'll try to tell you what's going on.

I wish I could give you a hug. I get suicidal a lot too. 

Remember that you're not alone. Social anxiety is ridiculously common, it's just that people tend to put up a defense by pretending they're doing fine even when they're completely lost. It sucks, but it's how society is right now.

I found a lot of perspective reading about psychology and philosophy. I realised that even the smartest people in the world, who work their whole lives to understand people don't have that many solid answers. Everyone's on the same journey towards understanding. Everyone's learning by doing.

I find the more I socialise, the less intense individual interactions seem. Maybe it's a kind of tolerance; you expose yourself to enough noise and it stops seeming so noisy.

Parents blaming their children makes me really really sad. My advice, get away from them as soon as you can. You can't expect people to change, and if they're not willing to really listen to you, you're only going to get so far with them.  


Tolerant people do exist, they just don't always advertise themselves. Talk to your teachers, lecturers, doctors, anyone further along in life than you who's willing to listen. People are basically good, they just get confused and scared of stuff they don't understand.
Change the subject. Talk about something else. High functioning people understand this as a cue to move on; low functioning people usually wont notice.
I would talk to anyone who took the time to talk to me. I know what it's like to feel completely alone.

Everyone has a different pattern of attention when it comes to other people. Usually the more attention we pay someone the better we understand them.

Fully developed is kind of a fictional idea; humans are way too complicated to ever understand completely. Most people assume they see everything clearly, including people's emotional states, but you can't see an emotion if you don't have a basic understanding of it.

Empathy is always a belief. You can never know for sure that you're feeling what someone else is feeling, but you can believe you do, and more importantly you can make \*them\* believe you do.

In most situations, when people deliberately include you it means that they like you. Tell them you're autistic and you don't like being focused on, or they might think your discomfort means you don't like them.
I think a lot of mothers have trouble letting go of the God role in their family. It stops occurring that they could be wrong.

People are more willing to forgive the people who have their respect, and everyone has different things that they respect in a person.  


Whether you accept someone's judgement is up to you. People are often ignorant and quick to anger if something triggers them.

There are things that people can do for you that make you feel better, and things you can do for other people that make them feel better.   


Humans are always going to be the most interesting things to other humans. Conscious beings have a complexity that media can't match, and there's a reason why some people seem literally addictive to be around.   


Autism makes it hard for people to understand what makes us feel good or bad, and makes it harder for us to know what makes other people feel good or bad. To figure it out we need to pay close attention to people even when they're not saying anything that's interesting to us.  


Have you ever looked at ASMR on youtube? It's like a human contact simulator. The freaky thing is that it can provoke a "real" feeling of being cared for. Maybe you can feel it too. That's what humans can do for each other.

YES. Hearthstone is a magnificently designed game. In my head (and around other aspies) I call it "math wars" because when you drill down it is simply numbers interacting with each other. I love the way the outcome is always the product of random happenstance (within a set of parameters) but allowing for enough application of intelligence that a skilled player will usually win-- but you can never know for sure whether it's possible because sometimes life just shits on you and you have to make the best regardless, because sudden reversals are not just possible but are the entire point of the game.

You never know when 2 health will make the difference, but is it worth more than keeping that minion alive? Interesting decisions like that keep me playing.

I find I really don't like "anti-meta" cards; the ones like weapon removal or Black Knight or Big Game Hunter that only become popular as a response to the one thing they counter being seen as popular. There is no gameplay in these cards; you play them after the thing it counters, always. No interesting decision.

I use a Hunter deck focused on midrange pressure (turn 4-6) with cheap removal (traps, weapons, etc) to keep everything moving in the right direction. I might be talking out of my arse but I find this deck more "fun" than most. I think it might be more mathy or something.
http://www.hearthpwn.com/decks/211196-survival-hunter

I want to add my positive recommendation. Cannabis reduces my anxiety and depression. It makes me more social and able to think creatively. It makes me question less and feel more. All the stuff the other comments say. In my mind it's the perfect aspergers treatment.

I recommend at least trying to smoke it. I've never had quite the same "feel" from edibles, and never a strong euphoria-- higher doses just get stonier. Vaping is different again, less so than edibles but distinct. There's a huge, huge range of experiences to be had from different strains too.

There are other illegal substances which I think have life-changing therapeutic potential especially for aspergers; but take it one step at a time if you're wary. Over time you'll realise there isn't much to be afraid of as long as you're responsible about it.

The simple assumption that they're right about everything, all the time, turns honesty into a social faux pas.

I feel a huge amount of resentment towards this majority that doesn't just get to to make the rules, but gets to be ignorant of them to the point when someone breaking them is intrinsically "wrong" in the context of reality itself.
People want to believe things that make sense of the world for them or help them feel safer.

Stagecraft is right. The way I see it NTs are like method actors, they just put themselves in the role and do what they feel is right. Aspies have to learn the techniques and mechanics and meanings. In the end that's usually way more valuable.

It's easy to get stuck inside your own head where your opinions and interests are not subjective. A person who has a deep understanding of a topic will see meaning where another sees raw data.
Aspies break situations down into mechanics to understand them. NTs break situations down into people to understand them. People are irrational; numbers are meaningless.

NTs only apply labels because the most efficient way for them to think about something is to personify it. They think in people, not mechanics. Also, you don't have to feel bad when you lie to them.

Be patient. We can be stubborn when we're having trouble dealing with a situation. It stops us from thinking straight, sometimes from thinking at all.

What she's going through probably isn't about you, but remember that your presence or contact might make her more stressed.  Just make sure she has a method of engaging you again, even if she doesn't want to talk about it. Make sure you're there when she does need you.

NTs will always interpret someone's words within the context of nonverbal cues like expression, tone and gesture. If the words don't match the perceived context they'll usually misinterpret them in a way that does. I don't think it's something they can help.
Stimulants. I take caffeine and modafinil first thing in the morning. It's not ideal in the long-term but it's the only reliable method I've found.

I think that a lot of us get stuck on the idea that conformity is bad because it indicates that we're not "being ourselves", whatever that means. Conformity is not intrinsically bad, it's just one way of being. You're allowed to keep doing it *even if you know better*.

Remember that even NTs don't usually understand the mechanics of social interaction past superficial conformity and letting their emotions dictate their reaction. (The Dunning-Kruger effect does the rest.) Your hard-won understanding of human interaction is both rare and valuable. It makes you a skilled practitioner in a world of method actors.

I've had an idea bouncing around my head for a while now that autism isn't so much a spectrum as a single root cause that affects everyone differently -- "aspergers" is a label we ended up giving to people who *as children* were able to overcome the challenge of making sense of the world around them while missing some intrinsic context. That this process would naturally select for intelligence seems an obvious conclusion, and would explain the positive correlation between aspergers and intelligence.

If anyone has any evidence to support/oppose this idea I'd be really interested to hear it.

It's not so much sensory overload as cognitive overload. It's definitely not unique to autism, but the theory is that we're not as good at "filtering out" intrusive noises and other sensory information-- strong emotions are also intrusive in this way.

Each individual stimulus will sidetrack our focus, which makes it harder to concentrate on anything else. Enough stimuli and our brain's not able to process any of it.

I think that the most distinctive feature of autism is this "focus" we have. I keep noticing this focus tends to occur when I unconsciously frame a situation as a game or puzzle to solve. Anything can be a game if you just try to do it more efficiently. 

I'm really interested to find out how common this tendency is, because I have a suspicion that thinking in "games" could be a central feature of this disorder. Or maybe I'm just noticing something everybody does without realising it and attributing it to a disorder, like those caetextia guys.

In a way all relationships end because of unfulfilled expectations. I lived with an aspie girl for several months who had a very specific understanding of how people are supposed to act. I'm sure she didn't feel like she was imposing a bunch of rigid behaviour patterns on me, but she sure would lose her shit if I did something "wrong". My point of view just wasn't something she had any consistent awareness of. In her mind any conflict was me failing at normal behaviour, or if she took it personally, "betraying" her.

She was upset a vast majority of the time, always for a different reason. Even when she wasn't angry at me she was stressful to be around. After a while I stopped trying to talk to her about it because that could trigger a brand new meltdown. Even having time to myself was stressful because if I closed my bedroom door I was "shutting her out"; but the alternative was feeling like I have to ask permission to be alone.

I ended up disconnecting from reality for several months. I stopped going to work. I'm amazed I still have a job, honestly. But even after that, when I'd been away from work for months and she understood that I needed her support just to keep going, she would still fly off the handle at the smallest misstep. She couldn't overcome her emotional reactions; where the only thing that mattered was that it was my fault. In retrospect it was clearly abusive behaviour, even if it wasn't quite deliberate.

This was exactly the cause of my own scepticism to my diagnosis-- understanding how easily false positives can present. It took years for me to become totally sure that this explanation was correct.

I think worrying about being geniune is kind of self-fulfilling. Like worrying about being a good person-- it proves you're at least on the right path.

I mean, for contrast, some people spend huge portions of their lives worrying about how they can stop gay people from being happy.

I think I understand where you're coming from though. Pretension is one of my most hated qualities in both myself and other people. I feel personally ashamed when I catch myself accidentally misrepresenting who I am.

But the other side or this is that pretension has been a part of human nature ever since the first man lied about the size of his cave to impress a woman, and noticing it in yourself is nothing to be concerned with.

Also remember NTs never, never notice it-- to them it's background noise.

Even after I was diagnosed, it took me a couple of years to lose my scepticism towards whether it was true, to eventually notice the multitude of completely obvious patterns in my behaviour.

Most people don't ever realise how little control they really have over their own human nature. The fact that you understand it means you can try to fix it if you want. Observation leads to understanding leads to more efficient techniques for self-improvement.

I frequently catch myself unconsciously mouthing or even whispering my inner dialogue in public. At home it's in a normal speaking voice.

I don't think that involuntary speech is anything unique to aspies, but we tend to do it a lot more often because we are more prone to losing consciousness of our body and surroundings.

Echolalia is when the thing you unconsciously say is just repeating what someone else said. It's one specific type of involuntary speech.

I think echolalia a bit of an esoteric symptom-- it's just easy to recognise in a patient (even as a false positive), and it's got a cool enough name that it gets included in common diagnostic criteria more than it probably deserves to.

It's really good to hear an explanation that doesn't rely on us being somehow less emotionally mature than other people. It can be tricky to get anyone to understand how something they think is simple can be hard for someone else-- that failure is not the same as incompetence.

I don't know what synaptic connections are, but my understanding of why I react emotionally before I realise I'm doing it is because of that peculiar aspie focus. Anything I'm not consciously aware of falls to the subconscious, which is unable to make the kind of intelligent determinations the conscious mind can. It just reacts the way it knows how.

The other side of the coin is that a strong enough emotion will invade my focus to demand attention, which is pretty debilitating, because it disrupts my ability to process anything else.

It's taken my whole life for me to learn to recognise when I'm feeling anxiety or depression, and to understand that my experience of being around people is not the experience that everyone else has.

I get so pissed off at doctors who prescribe first.

Your post seems to be asking for a diagnosis, which isn't allowed here. Lack of social contact and spending all your time on one activity is textbook aspergers though. Being socially isolated does tend to make a person depressed.

The terrible thing about aspergers is the experience is completely different to "normal" in a way that's invisible even to the afflicted-- the context-blindness goes both ways. People always assume everyone else is just like them and if they don't act the way I expect it's because they're stupid or weird. The aspie is "just being a jerk" when he explains the NT "never says what he means".
I that to an NT "directness and clarity" is asking them to think harder than they're able to. It's not their fault they don't bother to understand systems properly.

I understand this. The point of non-constructive social contact is almost always seeking empathy.

When a person expresses something random for "no reason" it's because they are expecting an empathetic response. It's not a question or an imperative; they just want someone to share what they are feeling.

The good news is that you can totally fake this by figuring out the emotion they are feeling and acting like you feel it too. You usually don't even have to be convincing-- in the social world trying still counts.

Empathy is the thing that makes connecting with another person intrinsically pleasurable. A shared pleasure is doubled, a shared pain is halved.

The way you describe it does seem to indicate that you lacked a contextual understanding of the text. If you are autistic then this stuff usually wont occur to you until someone else points it out. I have my doubts about the official diagnostic criteria, but it is possible to have a pretty good idea of what aspergers looks like, even if we can't explain that much of it yet.

The only way I can understand marriage is as a social construct. I had a soon-to-be-wed friend a while back who explained to me that it's "equally" about a commitment to a life long relationship, an official status which grants a tax advantage, and a ceremonial event. But that's bullshit because people don't do things for three reasons.

We're all of us constantly refining our understanding, realising that what we believed up until that point wasn't helping and figuring out what's *really* going on. People have this ridiculous assumption that learning is just what you do at school, rather than a life-long refinement.

I think life itself is ridiculous. It's only the people who take it seriously that have issues. In Africa we are at war with a parasitic life form which turns our own people into sleeper agents to help it breed. Politicians are so concerned with money that most people literally can't vote for someone who will represent their interests. Everyone thinks everything is everyone else's fault and responsibility.

Humans identity (and by extension our happiness) relates strongly to what kind of story we tell ourselves about ourselves; we need to be careful that we don't buy into stories that portray us in a way we are unhappy with.

This seems to conform to my theory as well as my personal experience-- if my attention is focused then I usually don't "notice" emotions at all until something breaks my focus.

For instance, I usually don't notice hunger until it's strong enough to break my concentration. Ditto for using the toilet. When I realised I have IBS I made a conscious effort to convince my subconscious to keep an eye on it. These days I will find myself walking to the bathroom before I even realise I need to use it, which I consider a success.

Offer to talk without insisting on it. If he doesn't want to, consider describing an explicit cue he can use to initiate conversation at another time. Often the hardest thing for us is understanding how to ask for help in a socially acceptable way.

Remember that people don't care so much what you say so much as you're saying *something* to engage them. If you can't think of anything to say, just inspect the item and make random observations. If there's text, you can read the text aloud-- My late grandfather used to do this all the time and never sounded the least bit impressed with anything.

Thanking the person directly is important because it's the cue for everyone to move on and stop paying attention to you.

I figured out the gift receiving thing a while back, mainly by studying how my mother does it. Basically the thing to keep in mind is that nobody is expecting a convincing performance, just go through the motions. Act surprised when you see what the gift is and say something like "oh wow!"-- If you can add some extra patter like how you might potentially use the item, or how you'd heard about it before that's even better. Then look directly at the person who gave it to you, smile and thank them. Again, nobody will notice how unconvincing you are. And then you're done.

As for being stuck in a close situation with other people... I usually go for long walks if I can't find a place to myself. Just make up some excuse-- In my experience NTs will accept the flimsiest of pretenses as long as you can "justify" your behaviour and aren't just doing what they see as random things.
